title: Pre-induction physical in Jacksonville
summary: He tries everything to fail his physical at his father's urging and is passed anyway.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I just was thinking about this, when I was sort of reading about you. And I saw the years you were in the service and I’m starting to wonder.

Okay. Now we’ll go in that direction. So now I’m down in Florida. And the pre-induction physical, I had to take it. So I took it in Florida. And my drinking chops have always been pretty up. In fact, do you mind if I prepare myself a little grape juice?
No, not at all. You go right ahead.
In fact if you’d like some more, there’s ice right here.
You know I’ve been thinking about those years a bit, because my Vietnam experience was more connected with the draft lottery. And I basically escaped because I got a high number.
Oh you didn’t go in the service?
I didn’t have to go, or, I didn’t.

Well the night that I — I took my pre-induction physical in Jacksonville, Florida. We were playing at the Cape Colony Inn which was owned, it was in Coco Beach, Florida, which was owned by the astronauts. And a trumpet player, Paul Squire drove me up there. My father said, “I’ve never wished you any bad luck in your life,” he says, “but now I hope you fail this one.” And man, I stayed up all night. We did every single thing we could put our hands on, including any controlled substance I could put my hands on, anything, to fail this exam. We drove up to Jacksonville, Florida wherever the physical was to take place, and I walked in and I mean I hadn’t slept, I hadn’t done anything except drink and get high and everything else. Here’s these muscle men, I mean these are Charles Atlas, Man Mountain, Montana guys. They say, “hey,” standing in line, I’d hear like, “Herman Slabonski.” “Yo!” You know, like, I’m right here. “Come on forward, we’ll check you out,” you know, this and that. So I mean all of these guys, and half of these guys are failing. I mean these guys are not — I don’t know if they’ve got a heart murmur, I don’t know what it is. And I’m standing there like, looked like Wally Cox you know, Mr. Peepers. Man, you don’t remember Wally Cox.

By the way, he happened to have been a war hero believe it or not. I mean you wouldn’t think so, you know, Mr. Peepers. So now I said, “how was that.” He said, “next.” You know like, he kept going down the line, man, instead of go to the back of the line like Herman Slabonski had to go to the back of the line and start over.
